analysis.one_liner: Banned members of Congress and staff from trading stocks on inside legislative information.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, the first version of what later became known as the STOCK Act, would have directed securities and commodities regulators to write rules barring anyone from trading stocks or futures while holding secret information about pending legislation obtained from a member or employee of Congress. It would have required members and staff to report their securities trades within 30 days, and required firms that sell political intelligence — advance word about congressional action sold to investors — to register and disclose their activities like lobbyists.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors, who would no longer be trading against members of Congress and well-connected firms that know what legislation is coming before the public does. The bill aimed to close a gap where information about pending laws could be used for private profit.

how_it_helps.text: Directed the SEC and CFTC to prohibit trading in securities or commodities futures by anyone possessing material nonpublic information about pending legislative action, whether obtained by being a member or employee of Congress or knowingly obtained from one.
Barred members and congressional employees from disclosing such nonpublic legislative information when they have reason to believe it will be used to trade.
Required members and legislative-branch officers and employees to report any securities transaction of $1,000 or more to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate within 30 days.

Brought political intelligence consultants and firms — intermediaries who sell advance knowledge of congressional action to investors — under the Lobbying Disclosure Act's registration, reporting, and disclosure requirements, with an exception for journalists gathering news.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their staff, who would lose the ability to trade on knowledge of pending legislation and would have to disclose their trades within 30 days; and political intelligence firms, whose business model would face registration and public disclosure for the first time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and political intelligence firms

drawbacks.text: The 30-day transaction reporting requirement would have imposed new paperwork on thousands of congressional employees, not just members, covering any trade of $1,000 or more.

Defining 'political intelligence contacts' broadly risked sweeping in legitimate policy analysis and market research; the bill carved out a media exception, but other analysts and trade associations would have faced registration and disclosure obligations for routine conversations with congressional staff.
The bill delegated the core trading ban to SEC and CFTC rulemaking within 270 days rather than writing the prohibition directly into law, leaving the exact scope of the ban to be set by regulators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — closing a loophole that allowed lawmakers and their contacts to profit from advance knowledge of legislation — is straightforward and aimed at restoring public confidence in Congress. The compliance burden on staff and the ambiguity around defining political intelligence were real but manageable design questions; nothing in the bill's substance explains why it never received so much as a committee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Baird introduced the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act on March 28, 2006, joined by Rep. Louise Slaughter as an original cosponsor.
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill: 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
On introduction day the bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the House Administration, Judiciary, and Agriculture Committees.
The action history shows no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referrals.
The 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill died with it without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and congressional staff kept the ability to trade securities without promptly disclosing their transactions, and political intelligence firms kept operating without registration or public disclosure. Anyone who profits from advance knowledge of legislative action was better off because the bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and political intelligence firms

for.name: Rep. Brian Baird
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the first congressional proposal to ban trading on knowledge of pending legislation and require rapid trade disclosure.

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill after it was referred; the bill sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary, House Administration, and Agriculture Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions within their jurisdiction; no committee reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor gathered 12 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors, but no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of any potential floor vote is unknown.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and congressional staff
industries.note: The bill would have barred them from trading on advance knowledge of legislation and required disclosure of their own trades within 30 days. Because the bill died without a vote, these rules never applied to them.

The bill would have required these firms — which sell advance word of congressional action to investors — to register and disclose their activities like lobbyists. Their business model depends on moving information that the public cannot see.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and institutional investors that buy political intelligence
industries.note: The bill would have barred trading while possessing nonpublic legislative information obtained knowingly from a member or employee of Congress, removing an informational edge over ordinary investors.
